title: Design Requirements and Specifications
description: Design requirements, the difference between needs and wants, quantitative and qualitative criteria, and writing a.
content_html:
What Are Design Requirements?

Before any design work begins, an engineer must establish what the product actually has to achieve. Design requirements are the full set of conditions the product must satisfy. They come directly from analysing the brief, researching the user, and understanding the context of use. Getting the requirements right is critical: a product that is beautifully made but fails to meet its requirements is a failed product, regardless of its technical quality.

Needs and Wants

Design requirements are divided into two categories. Needs are non-negotiable: they are the essential criteria without which the product simply cannot fulfil its purpose. A bicycle helmet needs to protect the user's head in a collision — that is a need. Wants are desirable but optional features that would improve the product without being essential — for example, the same helmet being available in multiple colours. In a specification, needs take priority over wants, and wants are usually only pursued if time and budget allow.

The distinction between needs and wants matters in the exam because you may be asked to classify a list of requirements or to argue why a particular criterion is a need rather than a want. Always justify your classification by referring back to the product's core function and the safety or performance consequences of omitting that feature.

Key Fact

Needs are essential — without them the product cannot fulfil its purpose or may be unsafe. Wants are desirable — they improve the product but their absence does not make it non-functional. In a design specification, needs must be satisfied before wants are considered. This hierarchy directly affects decisions about cost, time and scope during the engineering design process.

Quantitative and Qualitative Criteria

Design specifications contain two types of criteria. Quantitative criteria are expressed as numbers or ranges that can be measured objectively — for example, "the product must weigh no more than 500 g" or "the handle must fit hands in the 5th to 95th percentile range." Quantitative criteria make it straightforward to test whether a prototype meets the specification: either the measurement passes or it does not.

Qualitative criteria describe characteristics that cannot easily be reduced to a number — appearance, feel, style, and user satisfaction. For example, "the product must have a professional appearance suitable for an office environment" is qualitative. Qualitative criteria are harder to test objectively and typically require user feedback or expert judgment. A strong specification contains both types: quantitative criteria ensure functional performance; qualitative criteria ensure the product meets user expectations that numbers alone cannot capture.

Consider a specification for a new children's stacking toy. Quantitative criteria might include: maximum dimension of any piece = 40 mm (choking hazard regulation), minimum compressive strength = 50 N, production cost per unit = under £1.80. Qualitative criteria might include: bright, primary colours that appeal to children aged 2–5; pieces that feel satisfying to click together; a design that parents perceive as durable and safe. Neither type alone is sufficient. A toy that passes all quantitative tests but looks unappealing will not sell; a toy that looks perfect but fails the strength test is unsafe. The combination of quantitative and qualitative criteria in the specification gives the design team clear, complete targets to design and test against.

The Design Specification and ACCESS FM

The design specification is the document that translates all the requirements — needs and wants, quantitative and qualitative — into a formal set of criteria that the design must meet. OCR R038 requires you to know that the ACCESS FM framework provides the standard structure for organising specification criteria: Aesthetics, Cost, Customer, Environment, Size, Safety, Function, Materials and Manufacturing.

Each heading prompts specific questions. Aesthetics: what must the product look, feel or sound like? Cost: what is the maximum unit production cost? Customer: who will use it and what are their needs? Environment: will it be used indoors or outdoors; are there temperature, moisture or corrosion constraints? Size: what are the maximum and minimum dimensions? Safety: what hazards must be mitigated; which regulations apply? Function: what must the product do and how well? Materials: what material properties are required (strength, flexibility, food-safe, etc.)? Manufacturing: how will it be made; in what quantities; are there process constraints?

Key Fact

ACCESS FM is used at two points in the iterative process: first, as a framework for analysing existing products during secondary research (covered in Lesson 2); and second, as the structure for writing the design specification. Knowing that the same nine headings serve both purposes — and being able to apply them in both contexts — is a frequently examined point in R038.

Using the Specification Throughout the Design Process

A design specification is not written once and forgotten. In the iterative process, the specification is a live reference document: every design idea is checked against it, every model is assessed against it, and every prototype is evaluated against it. When a prototype fails to meet a criterion, the designer knows exactly what to change. When all criteria are met, the designer has evidence that the product is a successful solution to the brief. This is why writing a precise specification — with measurable criteria where possible — is so important: vague criteria produce vague evaluation and no clear basis for decision-making.

Weak specification criteria are a common source of lost marks. "The product must be strong" is too vague to test — replace it with "the product must withstand a compressive force of at least 150 N without permanent deformation." "The product must look nice" cannot be evaluated — replace it with "the product must have a finish that users in a target focus group rate as aesthetically appropriate for a professional office environment." In exam questions that ask you to write or improve specification criteria, always aim for precision: include a number or a testable condition wherever possible, and name the ACCESS FM heading the criterion belongs under.
exam_tip_html: When asked to write specification criteria in an exam, use ACCESS FM headings to organise your answer and make at least two of your criteria quantitative (include a number, measurement or range). Always distinguish needs from wants if the question asks you to prioritise — state what the product must do (need) before what it could do (want). A common error is to write the same type of criterion repeatedly under different headings; aim for variety across Aesthetics, Function, Size, Safety and Cost at a minimum.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Design requirements are divided into needs (essential, non-negotiable) and wants (desirable but optional), and into quantitative criteria (measurable numbers) and qualitative criteria (descriptive characteristics that require user judgment to evaluate).
  • The design specification translates all requirements into precise, testable criteria organised under the nine ACCESS FM headings — Aesthetics, Cost, Customer, Environment, Size, Safety, Function, Materials and Manufacturing.
  • The specification is used throughout the entire iterative process to guide design decisions and to evaluate models and prototypes — a precise specification with quantitative criteria enables clear, evidence-based evaluation.

glossary_terms.definition: The conditions a product must satisfy in order to be considered a successful solution to the design brief, divided into needs and wants.
Essential requirements that a product must meet in order to function correctly and satisfy the brief — non-negotiable criteria.
Specification criteria expressed as measurable numbers or ranges — for example, a maximum weight of 500 g or a minimum load bearing of 200 N.

A detailed document that translates the design brief and research findings into precise, testable criteria organised under standard headings, used to guide and evaluate the design throughout the iterative process.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a quantitative specification criterion?
A) The product must have a professional appearance
B) Users must find the product easy to hold
C) The product must weigh no more than 350 g
D) The product must look modern and stylish
practice_questions.marks: C) The product must weigh no more than 350 g [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a 'need' and a 'want' in a design specification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining a need (a need is an essential requirement without which the product cannot fulfil its purpose or may be unsafe). 1 mark for defining a want (a want is a desirable but optional feature that would improve the product but is not essential to its core function). Accept equivalent wording. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a design specification should include both quantitative and qualitative criteria.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that both types are needed (e.g. 'neither type alone is sufficient'). 2 marks for explaining what each type adds (e.g. 'quantitative criteria are measurable and allow the designer to objectively test whether the prototype passes or fails; qualitative criteria capture aspects such as aesthetics and user satisfaction that cannot be reduced to a number'). 3 marks for a fully developed explanation that links both types to the design process (e.g. 'together they give the design team complete targets: quantitative criteria ensure functional performance, while qualitative criteria ensure the product meets user expectations that numbers alone cannot describe — both are needed to evaluate the design fairly'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A designer is writing a specification for a new portable outdoor camping stove. Describe two specification criteria the designer should include, using the ACCESS FM framework. For each criterion, state which ACCESS FM heading it falls under.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per criterion (1 mark for a clearly stated criterion; 1 mark for correctly identifying the ACCESS FM heading and briefly explaining why it is relevant to this product). Example acceptable answers: Safety — the stove must meet BS EN 521 standards for portable appliances using liquefied petroleum gas, to ensure it does not create a fire or explosion risk in outdoor use (2 marks). Size — the stove must fold to no larger than 150 mm × 100 mm × 40 mm when packed, so that it fits inside a standard day-pack (2 marks). Accept any two well-reasoned criteria with correct ACCESS FM headings. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A design team is writing the specification for a new ergonomic office chair aimed at people who spend more than six hours per day at a desk. The client has stated that the chair must be both functional and visually appealing.

Discuss why it is important for the specification to include both needs and wants, and both quantitative and qualitative criteria.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion that explains the distinction between needs and wants with examples applied to the chair (e.g. adjustable lumbar support = need; fabric colour choice = want) and between quantitative and qualitative criteria (e.g. seat height adjustable 400–520 mm = quantitative; fabric must feel premium to professional users = qualitative). The discussion explains how both pairs of concepts work together to produce a complete, testable specification, and acknowledges potential tensions (e.g. wants may have to be sacrificed if the cost budget is tight; qualitative criteria are harder to test objectively). Both benefits and limitations are addressed.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least one example each of a need and a want, and at least one each of a quantitative and qualitative criterion, with some explanation of why both are included — but may lack balance or depth.
Developing (2 marks): The terms are used but not clearly explained or applied to the chair scenario.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A company is designing a new range of children's bicycle helmets for ages 5–10. The design team has written an initial specification using the ACCESS FM framework, but the project manager says the criteria are too vague to be useful for evaluating prototypes.

Evaluate the importance of writing precise, measurable specification criteria and consider whether there are any situations where qualitative criteria are unavoidable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing that precise, measurable (quantitative) criteria are essential because they allow objective pass/fail testing of prototypes against the specification, cite specific examples relevant to the helmet (e.g. impact absorption standard in joules, mass limit in grams, retention system release force in Newtons), and that vague criteria lead to subjective and inconsistent evaluation. The response then addresses the counter-argument: some criteria genuinely cannot be quantified — the appearance of a children's helmet must appeal to children and parents, and this can only be assessed through user testing and focus groups, making qualitative criteria unavoidable in any real specification. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached about how to handle the balance, supported by the helmet scenario. Quality of written communication is high.
Secure (5–6 marks): The importance of quantitative criteria is clearly argued with at least two examples, qualitative criteria are acknowledged as necessary for some aspects, and an attempt at a judgement is made — but the counter-argument may be underdeveloped.
Developing (3–4 marks): Both types of criteria are discussed but mainly described rather than evaluated, or the argument is largely one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about specifications with little or no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a 'need' rather than a 'want' when designing a children's bicycle helmet?
options: Available in a range of bright colours
Meets the impact protection standard EN 1078
Has a matching chin strap in a contrasting colour

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is an example of a qualitative specification criterion?
options: The product must have a finish that users perceive as professional and modern
Product dimensions must not exceed 200 mm × 150 mm × 50 mm

knowledge_checks.q: In the ACCESS FM framework, the 'C' for Customer prompts the designer to consider who will _____ the product and what their specific needs and preferences are.
A specification criterion that states 'the product must weigh no more than 500 g' is an example of a _____ criterion because it can be measured objectively.
Match each specification criterion to the correct ACCESS FM heading.
left: The product must not exceed a unit production cost of £8.50
The product must withstand outdoor temperatures from -10°C to +50°C
All sharp edges must be removed to prevent user injury

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a 'need' and a 'want' in a design specification?
flashcard_questions.a: A need is an essential requirement that the product must meet in order to fulfil its purpose safely and correctly, whereas a want is a desirable but optional feature.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a quantitative specification criterion?
flashcard_questions.a: A quantitative specification criterion is one that is expressed as a measurable number or range — for example, stating that the product must weigh no more than 350 g.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a qualitative specification criterion?
flashcard_questions.a: A qualitative specification criterion describes a characteristic that cannot easily be measured as a number — for example, that the product must have an appearance that users perceive as.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the ACCESS FM framework stand for?
flashcard_questions.a: ACCESS FM stands for Aesthetics, Cost, Customer, Environment, Size, Safety, Function, Materials and Manufacturing — nine headings used to structure a design specification and to analyse existing products.

flashcard_questions.q: At which two points in the iterative design process is ACCESS FM used?
flashcard_questions.a: ACCESS FM is used during the research stage to analyse existing or competitor products, and again during specification writing to organise the product criteria under the nine standard headings.

flashcard_questions.q: Why should a design specification include quantitative criteria wherever possible?
flashcard_questions.a: Quantitative criteria should be included wherever possible because they can be tested objectively against a measured result, making it clear whether a prototype passes or fails each criterion without.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are qualitative criteria still necessary in a design specification despite being harder to test?
flashcard_questions.a: Qualitative criteria are necessary because some important product characteristics — such as aesthetics, perceived quality and user comfort — cannot be captured by numbers alone and can only be.

flashcard_questions.a: The design specification provides a set of precise, testable criteria that the design team checks every design idea, model and prototype against throughout the iterative process, giving clear evidence.
